title: Tamsin and the Horizon
premise: Mara Kavanagh, caretaker of Earth's abandoned seed vault, is the last courier running the silent route between Earth and the colony world Horizon, which severed contact decades ago after an 'accident' no one will discuss. When Horizon's children — including a girl named Tamsin who claims to remember a life she never lived — begin sharing an identical dream of a massacre, Mara discovers their minds are carrying erased memories of the colony's founding generation. To prove what happened, he must smuggle Tamsin and the dream-children's testimony past the corporate archive that rewrote history, while his own fading memories reveal he was there on the night it happened. In the end, Mara sacrifices his remaining memories to restore the children's truth to the record, and Tamsin, carrying both his story and her own, reopens the route between the worlds.
about_author: Silas Kavanagh is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing disputed historical records before turning to fiction. He writes from a coastal town where the fog rolls in like something trying to be remembered.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. He pilots the courier vessel between Earth's dead seed vault and the silent colony Horizon, delivering supplies no one thanks him for and letters no one answers. The emotional beat is loneliness worn smooth into routine — until he receives an unscheduled transmission: a child's voice asking for him by name.

chapters.title: Children of the Same Dream
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On Horizon, eleven-year-old Tamsin describes the dream she and forty other children share nightly: fire in the lower hab rings, adults screaming names that aren't in any registry. The colony's administrators dismiss it as mass hysteria. Tamsin's beat is defiant wonder — she knows the dream is real because she can smell the smoke when she wakes.

chapters.title: Arrival at Horizon
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. He lands under cold official welcome; Administrator Voss insists the children's dreams are a viral neurological event and quietly schedules them for 'treatment.' Mara meets Tamsin, who describes his childhood home on Earth — a place he never told anyone. The beat is dread blooming beneath courtesy.

chapters.title: What the Records Say
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with archival interludes. He digs into Horizon's public history: the founding generation died in a reactor accident, all records agree, all records identical down to the typo. He finds Tamsin's 'impossible' memories match details redacted even from him. The beat is the vertigo of realizing the lie is institutional, not personal.

chapters.title: The Night Mara Forgets
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, fractured memory sequences. Under Tamsin's dream-link, his suppressed memories surface: he was a junior technician the night the founders were purged, and he ran rather than testify. The beat is shame — the discovery that his amnesia wasn't inflicted by others but chosen by his younger self.

chapters.title: Treatment
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The administrators begin erasing the children's shared dream through 'therapy,' and one by one the kids go quiet and smiling and empty. Tamsin resists by anchoring herself to Mara's memories, which now live inside the link. The beat is terror and tenderness entwined — she is becoming the keeper of a man's guilt.

chapters.title: The Vault Beneath
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Mara and Tamsin find the physical archive hidden beneath the seed vault's Earth terminus: raw recordings of the massacre, sealed by the corporation that still owns Horizon. Voss's enforcers track them there. The beat is desperate triumph curdling into pursuit — truth found, but not yet safe.

chapters.title: Voss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Cornered, Voss offers Mara a deal: destroy the recordings and receive restored, painless memories of his old life — or keep the truth and watch the children's treatment become permanent. Mara sees his own cowardice offered back to him, gift-wrapped. The beat is temptation rendered almost kind.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. Mara chooses the children over himself: he uploads the massacre recordings through the courier network, broadcasting them to both worlds, then surrenders his own memories as payment for the link that shields the children during the upload. Tamsin holds the connection open, whispering his name so someone remembers him. The beat is sacrifice as authorship.

chapters.title: Tamsin and the Horizon
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. A year later, the route between worlds has reopened; the founders are mourned, the children healed, and Mara lives quietly on Horizon, remembering nothing but trusting the girl who tells him who he was. Tamsin begins writing it all down. The beat is bittersweet renewal — memory survives by being handed to someone new.
